one_line: A shop counter with a clock on it: every screen is one thumb-reach from the bag, every stock state is written as a time, and the only thing moving on the page is time running out.
big_idea:
The organising idea is **time as inventory**. What OUR TIME actually sells is not cotton, it is a window — a drop opens, a drop closes, and the sizes that went are gone. So the site never *decorates* with clocks; it uses time as the data type for commerce. Stock is expressed as time. Sold-out is expressed as a timestamp ("SOLD OUT — 23:14, SUN 12 OCT"). Dispatch is expressed as a deadline ("order in 3h 12m for dispatch today"). The drop itself is not a date, it is a **range**: DROP 001 · 11:00 FRI → 23:00 SUN. Every single one of those is a proven conversion device *and* a proven brand device, which is how restraint and commerce stop fighting.

Three consequences follow, and they are the whole design.

**1. The counter is the nav.** The floating glass pill carries the live drop counter and the live bag. It is the most-looked-at object on the site and it is doing two jobs that both make money. Corteiz's inversion is the model — the timer counts to the drop **closing**, not opening, because "you have this long" converts and "wait" does not. It never hard-sells; it just states a fact that happens to be urgent. And because the counter is in the nav, it is on every screen of the funnel, including the cart drawer, without a single extra banner.

**2. The product is the hero asset.** The brief wants AI video and 3D flair. The commercially honest place to spend it is not an abstract atmosphere film — it is the **hourglass back-print on the navy tee, with the sand falling as you scroll**. One scroll sequence, locked-off, back view, and the thing animating is the graphic you are selling, printed on the garment you are selling, on a body so you can read the oversized fit. It is the hero, the brand metaphor, the product shot and the fit guide in a single asset. That is the opposite of decorative motion: remove it and you lose product information.

**3. "OUR TIME" is the arrival; "EARN EVERY SECOND" is the grind — and the site runs the arc in that order.** The grind copy lives on the counter and the cutoff (pressure, urgency, work). "OUR TIME." lands once, at the end, over the crew shot, as the payoff. It is a *we* brand: the list is "THE LIST", the drop is "ours", sold-out copy is "gone in 4h 12m — that was quick, thank you", never "you missed it". Collective, not lone-wolf hustle.

Why this fits OUR TIME specifically and not any streetwear brand: the palette is already the most restrained in the category (the loudest thing the brand owns is a muted slate, #54647E), the motifs are literally timekeeping instruments, and the range is small and colour-driven. A small, colour-driven range wants a *bar of washes you tap through*, not a filter panel. A brand whose whole metaphor is a countdown wants a drop mechanic, not an always-on catalogue. The commerce architecture and the brand concept are the same architecture. That is why it will not read as a template: templates bolt a theme onto a shop; here the theme *is* the shop's data model.

art_direction.palette:
All values measured from the supplied renders, not invented. Tokens are named after materials, never `--primary`/`--accent` (tell #7).

**Grounds**
- `--ot-ground: #0F0F0F` — the page. The textured near-black from the tee render. **Never `#000000` as a surface.**
- `--ot-void: #000000` — reserved *inside imagery only*, as the photographic backdrop. Never a CSS background.
- `--ot-paper: #DFDDDE` — the light ground (off-white). Used for the Fit & Care section, the size guide, and the washed-black product's context.

**Ink**
- `--ot-bone: #FAF6F6` — primary type on dark. Slightly warm; **not `#FFF`**. 19.1:1 on `#0F0F0F`.
- `--ot-ink: #0F0F0F` — type on `--ot-paper`.
- `--ot-quiet: #A7A5A4` — secondary type, sold-out strikes, legends. 7.9:1 on ground. This is the *washed grey short*, so the UI's grey is literally a garment colour.

**Garments (also the colour bar swatches)**
- Navy tee `#141B2C` · navy short `#141925` · washed black `#171717` · washed grey `#A7A5A4` · washed denim `#54647E` · off-white `#DFDDDE` · cream/sand `#CFC2B4`.
- **Hard rule:** washed black `#171717` is only 8 points off the page ground. It must never be presented on `--ot-ground`. Every washed-black product frame, swatch and card sits on `--ot-paper` `#DFDDDE`. This single rule stops the darkest SKU from disappearing, and it is exactly the kind of decision no template makes.

**The one accent — and its licence**
- `--ot-live: #54647E` (washed denim). It is the brand's most saturated colour, so introducing any other hue would instantly become the loudest thing OUR TIME owns. We introduce none. `#54647E` is allowed **only to mark time-and-stock truth**: the 2px rule under the live counter, the low-stock hairline on a size chip, the focus ring, the cart-line quantity stepper's active state. It is never a button fill, never a link colour, never decoration.
- Measured: `#54647E` on `#0F0F0F` is **3.2:1** — passes the 3:1 UI-component/large-text floor, **fails body text**. So it is never body-size text on dark. On `--ot-paper` it is 5.4:1 and may be used as text there. This is written into the token file as a comment.

**No red anywhere on the site.** Sold-out is `--ot-quiet` with a strike. Errors are bone text on a `#171717` chip with a 2px `--ot-live` left rule plus an inline word ("Sold out in M" / "Code not valid"), never colour alone. Removing red from an e-commerce site is a deliberate, slightly uncomfortable decision — and it is the single clearest signal that the palette came from the garments and not from Tailwind.

**Derived UI tokens**
- `--ot-hairline: rgb(250 246 246 / .14)` · `--ot-hairline-strong: rgb(250 246 246 / .28)`
- `--ot-scrim: rgb(15 15 15 / .78)` (the nav contrast floor — see glass)
- `--ot-rim: rgb(250 246 246 / .38)`
- Radius: **0 everywhere, except the nav pill and the swatch dots, which are full pills.** Stüssy's `0` or Palace's max-int — commit to a pole, never the polite 8–16px middle (tell #22).
art_direction.typography:
Two faces, three weights, one italic. The brand's own typographic signature is a contrast pair — heavy sheared italic monogram against a thin, very widely letterspaced wordmark — so the site reproduces that tension rather than inventing a third voice.

**PRIMARY — Söhne (Klim Type Foundry).** Weights: **Söhne Buch (400)** and **Söhne Kräftig (600)**. Plus **Söhne Mono Buch** for the counter and prices only.
- *Licensing:* Klim sells a one-off, perpetual webfont licence banded by monthly pageviews; the entry band is appropriate for a launch storefront and is a few hundred pounds for the three styles. Self-host `.woff2`, `font-display: swap`, `unicode-range` subset to Latin. No Adobe Fonts / no Google Fonts CDN — a third-party font CDN is both a render-blocking third party and a soft tell.
- *Why Söhne:* it is the grotesque proven in exactly this register (Aimé Leon Dore ship it), it has a genuinely good mono sibling, and its slightly squared terminals sit correctly next to the OT monogram's angular cuts.

**ALTERNATE 1 — Akkurat (Lineto), Light + Bold.** The Cole Buxton stack; closest positional match to OUR TIME. Lineto web licence is a one-off per style. Choose this if the client prefers a cooler, more Swiss read.

**ALTERNATE 2, ZERO BUDGET — a system grotesque stack:** `font-family: "Helvetica Neue", Helvetica, -apple-system, "Segoe UI", Arial, sans-serif` with `font-synthesis: none`. This is genuinely what Stüssy and Palace effectively ship, it costs nothing, it is 0 KB, and it is *more* credible than any Google font. **Inter, Poppins, Montserrat, DM Sans, Manrope, Space Grotesk, Plus Jakarta Sans and Geist are banned by name** (tells #8–9; Trapstar and Kith are real, major brands whose sites read as templates for exactly this reason).

**THE WORDMARK — the fragile part, and the rule that protects it.**
"OUR TIME" is two words, seven letters, set thin and very widely letterspaced. The word space collapses to "OURTIME" the moment anything is left to a default.
- **Primary rule: the wordmark ships as inline SVG from the real vector, never as live text.** Two instances on the entire site — the footer lockup and the intro/loading state — and nowhere else. Its scarcity is what makes it read as a mark rather than a style.
- Where live text is unavoidable (the `<title>`, `alt`, `og:title`, the About page's one large setting), it is protected explicitly and never inherited:
```css
.ot-wordmark {
  font-family: "Sohne", sans-serif; font-weight: 400;
  text-transform: uppercase;
  letter-spacing: 0.34em;
  word-spacing: 0.62em;      /* explicit. never a default. */
  white-space: nowrap;
  padding-right: 0.34em;     /* reclaim the trailing track */
}
```
  `word-spacing` is set as a real value, not `normal`; the space is a real U+0020, never ` ` (which some engines will not expand); and there is a Playwright assertion in CI that measures the rendered gap between the R and the T and fails the build if it is under 0.5em. That test is the un-vibe-coded detail — a build gate protecting a kerning decision.
- **The wordmark is never a headline.** It never stretches to 100vw across a hero (tell #11 and the single most obvious move available).

**THE INVERTED TRACKING RULE (from Aimé Leon Dore, and it is the whole game).** Tight and large, or tiny and wide-tracked. Never both.

| Role | Size | Weight | Tracking | Case |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Display | `clamp(2.5rem, 7.2vw, 5.25rem)` | Kräftig | **-0.02em** | UPPER |
| Section head | `clamp(1.375rem, 3vw, 2rem)` | Kräftig | -0.01em | UPPER |
| Product title | `1.0625rem` | Kräftig | 0 | Sentence |
| Body / description | `1rem` / 1.55 | Buch | 0 | Sentence |
| Price | `1rem` Söhne Mono | Buch | 0 | — |
| **Micro-label** | **0.625rem (10px)** | Buch | **0.15em** | UPPER |
| Nav item | 0.6875rem (11px) | Buch | 0.12em | UPPER |
| Counter digits | `clamp(1.75rem, 5vw, 3rem)` Söhne Mono | Buch | 0 | — |
| Counter legends | 0.625rem | Buch | 0.15em | UPPER |

The 10px/0.15em micro-label is where the brand's wide-tracked look actually belongs: size chips, sold-out tags, drop names, `EST. 2026`, filter labels, the free-shipping threshold. It is a label attached to an object, never a decorative eyebrow above every section (tell #12).

**Numerals.** `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` on every price, counter and quantity — so digits do not jitter as the counter ticks and prices align down the cart. The garment-measurement table uses `font-variant-numeric: diagonal-fractions` so `20½"` sets properly. One line of CSS; no template contains it.
art_direction.imagery:
**The shot language, stated as a rule: the camera is behind or beside the wearer, not in front of them.** ~80% of frames are back, three-quarter-away, or cropped at the jaw. This is simultaneously (a) the strongest streetwear film language, (b) the reason the hourglass back-print reads as the hero, and (c) the single most reliable way to dodge the AI-face tells — plastic skin, symmetrical features, glassy eyes (tell #47). It reads as art direction, not as a limitation, because the product genuinely lives on the back of the tee.

**Light.** One large soft north-light source from camera left, hard falloff to near-black on the right, **no fill, no rim light, no hair light**. Overcast, 5200K, matte. Shot on 35mm, fine grain, slight halation in the highlights, matte blacks that never reach #000 in the frame. Explicitly stated in every prompt as a physical description — "single large soft key from camera left, hard shadow falloff, no fill" — never as a mood word like "cinematic" or "moody".

**Two environments, and only two.**
1. **The studio** — `#0F0F0F` textured seamless, matching the supplied flat-lays exactly, so AI on-model frames and real flat-lays cut together in one PDP gallery without a seam. This is the majority.
2. **One real place** — a wet, overcast British street at blue hour: kerb, wet tarmac, a shuttered unit, sodium light off frame. Never golden hour, never a rooftop, never neon. Used for exactly three frames on the whole site (the closing crew shot and two collection headers).

**Casting.** Two models, adults 20s–30s, faces deliberately unremarkable (distinctive faces date a campaign and drift more). Built for oversized fits: one tall/lean, one broader. Faces approved by the client *before* the full set is generated — the 5-view character sheet is frozen and reused as fixed inputs on every subsequent call, forever.

**The product-truth rule, which is also the legal position.** Every generated frame is QA'd against the real flat-lay in `brand/source/` for: print position, print scale relative to the collar seam, wash mottle, seam placement, ribbing, drawstring, drape. The model's jawline is not why anyone buys a tee; misrepresenting the *garment* is the only real exposure. UK ASA has no blanket AI-disclosure rule — the test is "is the audience likely to be misled" — so the operative control is product accuracy, plus a quiet footer line: *"Campaign imagery made with AI. Every garment shown is a real product, in a real colourway."* That line is a trust signal, not an apology.

**Banned in every prompt, expressed positively (Gemini has no negative channel — saying "no extra logos" reliably produces extra logos).** Instead: "The frame contains: one person, the garment, the seamless backdrop. Plain garment surfaces apart from the specified print. Unbranded footwear. Natural matte skin with visible pores and texture. Hands resolved, five fingers per hand, relaxed at the sides."

**Flat-lays stay.** They are the grid's second hover image and the PDP's detail tiles. Product shown *only* as flat-lay is tell #50; product shown only on models loses the garment-dye detail that is the actual product. Both, in a fixed rhythm: card = on-model, hover = flat-lay.
art_direction.motion:
**There are exactly four motion behaviours on this website. Anything not on this list does not move.**

**1. The counter ticks.** One second, one step, tabular digits, no easing, no flip animation, no odometer roll. It is an instrument reading, not an effect. When it hits zero it does not show `00:00:00:00` — it swaps in place for a live link (Cole Buxton's `onceItEnds` behaviour, and the `:has()` visibility guard below prevents the flash of zeros on first paint):
```css
.hero__copy:has(.ot-counter[data-state="resolving"]) { visibility: hidden; opacity: 0; }
```

**2. Media crops open.** Reveals are a `clip-path: inset()` opening from 6% to 0 over **480ms** with `cubic-bezier(.16,.84,.30,1)` — a crop, not a fade-up-translate. Ships as native `animation-timeline: view()` behind `@supports`, with a 15-line `IntersectionObserver{once:true}` fallback for Firefox. **No stagger.** Everything in a row opens together. Staggered 100ms increments are tell #38, and an unstaggered simultaneous crop reads as a shutter, which is on-brand.

**3. The specular rakes.** The nav pill's rim highlight angle is a registered custom property driven by scroll progress — one full 360° sweep over the length of the page, so the highlight crosses the rim like a second hand crossing a watch face. `@property --ot-light { syntax:'<angle>'; inherits:false; initial-value:210deg; }`, updated once per rAF from a passive scroll listener already running for the nav's other jobs. Zero extra cost, works in every engine, frozen flat at 210deg under `prefers-reduced-motion`.

**4. The hourglass scrubs.** One canvas image sequence, one pinned section, on the homepage only. Covered under imagery and tech.

**The single spring, and it is a commerce event.** Add-to-bag. The nav pill does one 520ms gel squash-and-stretch and the bag count increments. Nothing else on the site springs — which is precisely what makes the add-to-bag feel like a transaction landing rather than a generic UI flourish.
```css
.ot-pill[data-just-added] { animation: ot-gel 520ms linear(0,.42 12%,.86 24%,1.06 36%,1.02 52%,.995 72%,1); }
```
(`linear()` easing support is flagged UNVERIFIED in the research; the failure mode is safe — an unparsed `animation-timing-function` degrades to `linear`, which still reads fine.)

**Restraint rules, written as a lint list for the build:**
- No custom cursor. No scroll-progress bar. No 3D tilt cards. No count-up numbers. No typewriter. No marquee of words carrying no information. (Tells #37–45.)
- No page-load intro animation except the one wordmark state, and that only on a cold first visit, gated on `sessionStorage`, and dismissable by any interaction.
- No hover state that changes nothing perceptible. Card hover = the flat-lay crossfades in over 220ms and the size chips appear. That is information, not flourish.
- **`prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` is wired for real**, not as a global `*` nuke bolted on at the end: the sequence renders one chosen frame at 62% progress, the counter still ticks (it is information, and SC 2.2.2 concerns decorative motion, not a data readout), video autoplay is removed and controls are shown, the specular freezes, and crops are replaced by instant visibility.
- Autoplaying hero video is `muted playsinline loop` with a **designed poster** and an explicit pause control in the corner — WCAG 2.2.2 Pause/Stop/Hide is Level A and is a real compliance item for a UK storefront, not a nicety.

page_by_page.name: 00 · THE PILL (persistent chrome)
page_by_page.purpose: The shop counter. Carries the live drop timer and the live bag on every screen of the funnel, and becomes the add-to-bag control on a PDP. This is the conversion engine disguised as the brand's prettiest object.
page_by_page.layout: **Desktop:** floating pill, centred, `top:20px`, max-width 560px, height 52px, full radius. Left: OT monogram SVG, 22px, as the home link. Centre: `SHOP` (opens a flyout, not a mega-menu), `THE LIST`. Right: the counter `02:14:09` in Söhne Mono with a 2px `#54647E` rule beneath, then `BAG (2)`. Eleven-px uppercase at 0.12em tracking. Five items, hard cap. **Mobile:** bottom-anchored, `bottom: calc(14px + env(safe-area-inset-bottom))`, inset 14px, height 54px. Contents reduce to `[OT] SHOP 02:14:09 BAG (2)`. **On a PDP, mobile and desktop:** the pill morphs — nav items slide out over 320ms and it becomes `[S][M][L][XL] · ADD — £48`, the size chips inline, sold-out sizes struck in `#A7A5A4` and not tappable.
page_by_page.media: None. The pill contains no imagery. This is deliberate: every pixel in it is either a control or a number.
page_by_page.interaction: Tier 2 glass with a 0.78 scrim floor. `IntersectionObserver` flips `data-over` between `dark`, `light` and `media` per section — inverting the token set over the bone sections, and opacity-cross-fading to an opaque pill over any video or the canvas sequence. The rim specular angle is driven from scroll progress, one full sweep per page, like a second hand. Scroll-down hides the pill with a 200ms translate; scroll-up brings it back (Cole Buxton's `sticky="scroll-up"`). Add-to-bag triggers the site's only spring — a single 520ms gel squash — and increments the count via `aria-live="polite"`. Tapping BAG opens the cart drawer; the pill stays visible above the drawer's blurred scrim.

page_by_page.name: 01 · THE COUNTER (hero)
page_by_page.purpose: Say what this is, say how long is left, and put a buyable product one tap away. Zero-scroll time-to-product.
page_by_page.layout: Full-bleed `100svh` (svh, not vh — the mobile URL bar must not cause a CLS event). The frame is the hero still/loop, cropped so the model's back and the hourglass print occupy the centre-right third. **Desktop:** copy block bottom-left, 64px gutter: micro-label `DROP 001 · 11:00 FRI → 23:00 SUN` at 10px/0.15em; under it the counter, `clamp(1.75rem,5vw,3rem)` Söhne Mono tabular, with legends `DAYS HOURS MINS SECS` at 10px/0.15em beneath each pair; under that a display line `TIME WON'T WAIT` at -0.02em; and a single text link `SEE THE DROP →`. Bottom-right, a 10px micro-label: `EST. 2026`. **No centred headline, no button pair** (tell #18). **Mobile:** the same block anchored bottom-left above the pill, counter drops to `1.75rem`, the display line drops out entirely — on a phone the counter *is* the headline.
page_by_page.media: H01 — the hero loop. 9:16 and 16:9 cuts of the same setup: model from behind in the navy `#141B2C` oversized washed tee, hourglass back-print filling the frame, standing still on the `#0F0F0F` seamless, fabric moving almost imperceptibly as if from a slow draught. Near-still — a photograph that happens to breathe.
page_by_page.interaction: One `

page_by_page.name: 02 · THE DROP (the rail)
page_by_page.purpose: Buy in two taps. This is the highest-value section on the site and it is the **second** thing you see — before any editorial, before the sequence.
page_by_page.layout: Full-width band on `--ot-ground`. A 10px micro-label header row: `DROP 001 — 7 PIECES` left, `SIZES S–XL` right, hairline rule between. **Desktop:** a 4-up grid, `aspect-ratio: 4/5` on each card, 2px gutters (not 24px — tight gutters read as a contact sheet, wide gutters read as a template). Card: on-model image, title in 17px Kräftig, price in Söhne Mono, and on hover the flat-lay crossfades in over 220ms while a row of size chips appears at the bottom edge. **Mobile:** 2-up grid, same ratio, same 2px gutter, size chips always visible (no hover on touch — never hide the conversion affordance behind a hover state). A tap on a size chip adds that variant directly; a tap on the image goes to the PDP.
page_by_page.media: P01–P07 — one on-model frame and one flat-lay per SKU. The tee on-model is a three-quarter-back; the six shorts are waist-to-mid-calf, no face in frame at all, on a body so the drape and the garment-dye mottle read. Flat-lays are the existing `brand/source/` renders, re-cropped to 4/5.
page_by_page.interaction: Quick-add from the card, which is near-universal in the category and is the single biggest grid-level conversion lever. Adding fires the pill's gel spring and increments the bag — the cart drawer does **not** auto-open (auto-opening drawers interrupt browsing and measurably reduce units per order). Sold-out sizes are struck in `#A7A5A4` and carry a 10px timestamp on the PDP. A size chip with `quantityAvailable <= 2` carries a 1px `#54647E` underline and nothing else — no "only 2 left!" banner, no fake urgency. Cards reveal with the 480ms crop-open, unstaggered.

page_by_page.name: 03 · THE HOURGLASS (the one scroll sequence)
page_by_page.purpose: The 3D flair, spent in the one place it reads as intentional: the back-print animating on the product. It is the brand metaphor and a fit demonstration in the same asset.
page_by_page.layout: A `250vh` section containing a `position: sticky; top:0; height:100svh` stage. Locked-off back view of the model in the navy tee, centred, print occupying roughly 45% of the frame height. **Desktop:** the frame sits in a 68vw centred column so the `#0F0F0F` ground bleeds either side, with a 10px micro-label pinned bottom-left that updates with scroll progress: `EARN EVERY SECOND` → `00:12` → `00:31` → `SAND'S GONE`. **Mobile:** full-bleed, and the section shortens to `180vh` so the scrub is 6–8px per frame and does not feel like it is fighting the thumb. The sequence ends resolving into a still frame with a single text link: `THE NAVY TEE — £48 →`.
page_by_page.media: S01 — a 96-frame WebP sequence. Built from **one** approved 4K Gemini still (back view, navy tee, hourglass print), with the sand level animated as a luma matte inside the print region, displaced by a Depth Anything V2 depth map of the tee so the sand line follows the fabric folds and breaks at the crease. Deterministic, ~£0 in API spend after the one still, and impossible to shoot — which is exactly what makes it read as art direction rather than a filter.
page_by_page.interaction: Canvas-drawn image sequence, **not** a scrubbed `

page_by_page.name: 04 · THE WASHES (colour bar)
page_by_page.purpose: Merchandise the six shorts colourways as colour, because a six-SKU colour-driven range wants a bar you tap through, not a filter panel. This is the range's whole commercial proposition in one screen.
page_by_page.layout: Split band. **Desktop:** left 58% is a single large on-model shorts frame, `aspect-ratio: 4/5`; right 42% is the wash list — six rows, each a 28px pill swatch in the measured hex, the name at 10px/0.15em (`WASHED DENIM`, `CREAM / SAND`…), the price, and a `SOLD OUT` strike where applicable. Active row carries a 2px `#54647E` left rule. Below, `ADD — £42` and a size row. **Mobile:** the frame is full-bleed `4/5` on top; the six swatches become a horizontal scrolling row of 44px pills beneath it (44px = the tap-target floor), with the active name and price under the row. Swiping the image also changes the wash.
page_by_page.media: C01–C06 — six frames, same model, same pose, same light, one variable changed. Generated from a single approved hero frame using virtual try-on or a single-variable Gemini edit, so the colourway grid is genuinely consistent rather than six loosely related pictures. **The washed-black `#171717` frame is shot on the `#DFDDDE` paper ground**, not the near-black — and its section carries `data-nav-theme="light"`, so the nav inverts as you reach it.
page_by_page.interaction: Tapping a swatch crossfades the frame over 180ms and updates the price, the size availability and the URL (`?colour=washed-denim`, shareable, and the canonical stays on the PDP). No carousel library — a scroll-snap row and a crossfade. This section is where the nav's adaptive tinting gets its most visible moment, because the ground genuinely changes colour under the pill.

page_by_page.name: 05 · FIT & CARE (the trust band)
page_by_page.purpose: Kill the #1 return driver on an oversized washed tee, pre-empt the #1 complaint on garment-dye, and carry the delivery/returns copy. Boring, load-bearing, and designed rather than dumped in an accordion.
page_by_page.layout: The only section on `--ot-paper` `#DFDDDE` with `#0F0F0F` ink. `data-nav-theme="light"`. **Desktop:** three columns, hairline rules between, no cards, no icons-in-circles (tell #25). Col 1 **FIT** — "Cut oversized. Take your usual size for the intended fit, or size down for a regular fit." plus the model line: *"Model is 6'1" / 185cm, chest 38" / 97cm, wearing M."* and a garment-measurement table (pit-to-pit, body length, shoulder) in tabular figures with `diagonal-fractions` so `20½"` sets properly. Col 2 **WASH** — "Garment-dyed and washed. Expect up to 3% shrinkage and slight colour variation between pieces. That is the process, not a fault. Cold wash, inside out, dry flat." Col 3 **DELIVERY & RETURNS** — UK £4.95 / free over £75, 2–3 working days; 14-day right to cancel, 30 days to return unworn with tags; the address and trading name. **Mobile:** stacked, hairline-separated, all open by default — **no accordions.** Hiding sizing behind a tap is a measured returns cost.
page_by_page.media: One frame only: a macro detail, `aspect-ratio: 2.4`, bleeding off both edges — the shorts waistband, drawstring aglet and washed grey seam at close range, on the paper ground. Tactile, no person, no logo.
page_by_page.interaction: Almost none, and that is the point. The one moving element is the dispatch cutoff, a second timer in a different register from the hero's: `ORDER IN 3H 12M FOR DISPATCH TODAY` at 10px/0.15em with the figure in Söhne Mono. Two timers, two jobs — that is what stops the countdown reading as a gimmick.

page_by_page.name: 06 · OUR TIME (the payoff)
page_by_page.purpose: The one emotional beat, and the only place the brand's name is spoken at scale. It arrives after the commerce, not before — which is what makes it land.

page_by_page.purpose: The last surface we fully control. Below Shopify Plus you cannot touch the checkout's information/shipping/payment steps, so the drawer has to carry the whole brand handoff — and it has to remove every remaining reason not to pay.

Lines: 72px thumbnail, title, `M / WASHED DENIM` at 10px/0.15em, a `−  1  +` stepper in tabular figures with `#54647E` on the active control, `REMOVE` as a 10px text link. time_theme:
**Time is the data type, not the decoration.** Four structural expressions, each of which also does commercial work:

**1. Stock is written as time.**
- `SOLD OUT — 23:14, SUN 12 OCT`. Not a grey badge, a timestamp. It tells a returning customer how fast it went, which is the most persuasive social proof a small brand has, and it costs nothing because the platform already stores it.
- Low stock is a 1px `#54647E` underline on the size chip. No "only 2 left!" banner, no fake scarcity — the scarcity is real and stated quietly.
- A `quantityAvailable` of `null` (untracked) renders as available with no count, never as zero. Tri-state, modelled from day one.

**2. The drop is a range, not a date.** `DROP 001 · 11:00 FRI → 23:00 SUN`. The counter counts to the **close**, following Corteiz's inversion — "you have this long" converts where "wait" does not. `data-timezone="store"` so it is one global moment, `onceItEnds` swaps the timer in place for a live collection link with no dead zeros, and a `:has()` visibility guard prevents the flash of `00:00:00` on first paint. It is content-managed (a metaobject, editable by the owner in Shopify admin) and never hardcoded — the single most common way a countdown becomes an embarrassment is that it expires and nobody can change it.

**3. Two timers, two registers — which is what stops it being a gimmick.** The hero counter is the *grind* (`EARN EVERY SECOND`, pressure, the window closing). The dispatch cutoff in the cart and the Fit & Care band is the *service* (`ORDER IN 3H 12M FOR DISPATCH TODAY`, calm, factual, a straight conversion lever). One countdown that shouts and one that reassures. A site with a countdown on every product has no scarcity, it has a Shopify app.

**4. The archive is the brand's proof, and it accrues.** Closed drops stay on the site at their own handles, every size struck, every sell-out timestamped, the counter replaced by `CLOSED 23:00, SUN 12 OCT · 7 PIECES · 4 SOLD OUT`. Nothing is deleted. After four drops the `/archive` route is a ledger of windows that opened and closed — the brand's history expressed as elapsed time. That is a real IA decision that only makes sense for a brand called OUR TIME, it is free to build (it is just the collection page with a closed state), and it is the payoff the concept has been earning the whole way down.

**And the narrative arc runs the name's two halves in order.** "EARN EVERY SECOND" and "TIME WON'T WAIT" live at the top, on the counter, in the grind. "OUR TIME." lands once, near the bottom, over the crew shot, as the arrival. Put in the overtime, and then it is our time. The copy is collective throughout — `THE LIST`, `gone in 4h 12m — that was quick, thank you`, never "you missed it", never a lone-wolf hustle register.

**What is deliberately excluded, because it is where this concept goes to die:** no ticking-clock cursor (four tells at once, breaks on touch, turns the idea into a joke), no live clock in the header, no hourglass loading spinner, no sand-particle canvas, no second-hand scroll-progress bar, no Roman numerals in UI, no CSS/SVG clock face as a hero graphic, and no tessellated OT monogram behind text. The hourglass, the clock face and the monogram pattern are *print on garments*. The moment one becomes a UI element it becomes the cliché the whole direction is trying to avoid. The single exception — the rim specular sweeping the nav pill once per page like a second hand — is allowed because it is invisible as a metaphor and only readable as craft.

tech_stack:
**Framework: Astro 5, SSR, TypeScript strict, deployed on Cloudflare Pages (Netlify equally fine).**

Why Astro and not Next/Hydrogen: the site is 90% static content with four genuinely interactive islands (the pill, the sequence, the PDP variant selector, the cart drawer). Astro ships zero JS by default and lets each island choose its own hydration directive — `client:idle` for the pill, `client:visible` for the sequence, `client:load` for the PDP buy column. That is the right shape for a site whose whole thesis is restraint, and it gets the JS budget under 45 KB gz excluding the one dynamic GSAP import.

Why **SSR and not static**: two hard reasons. (1) Product pages must be server-rendered for `Product` JSON-LD and indexable PDPs — a client-only SPA storefront is an SEO own-goal. (2) If site content moves to Shopify **metaobjects** (the announcement bar, the drop window, the homepage section order — the things the non-technical owner needs to change himself), those require the *private* Storefront token, which is server-only. Choosing static now would force a re-platform the moment he wants to edit the countdown himself. Decide it up front.

**Hydrogen and Oxygen are explicitly rejected.** They are the maximum-lock-in option, the framework has been rewritten under its users twice (RSC → Remix → React Router), the "free hosting" is worth £0–16/month, and they give nothing that this stack doesn't. They also cannot be started before the platform is confirmed, which is disqualifying today.

**THE COMMERCE SEAM — this is the load-bearing decision.**

```
components/ ──▶ useCommerce() ──▶ StorefrontAdapter ──▶ local-json | shopify | stripe
            ──▶ useContent()  ──▶ ContentAdapter    ──▶ local-json | metaobjects
```

Seven rules that make the seam real rather than aspirational:
1. No Shopify type and no `gid://shopify/...` string ever appears in a component. IDs are opaque branded strings (`ProductId`, `VariantId`, `CartLineId`).
2. Money is never a JS `number` in the UI — `{ amountMinor: 4800, currencyCode: "GBP" }` and one `formatMoney()`.
3. URLs key on **handle**, never on ID.
4. The front end never computes tax, shipping or totals. It renders what the cart returns. `cost.tax` is `null` until the platform knows, and the UI says "calculated at checkout" rather than inventing a figure.
5. Exactly one file knows the API version string (`SHOPIFY_API_VERSION = "2026-07"`). Bumping it quarterly is a ~1-hour job in one constant.
6. Adapters return typed results for user-visible failures (`{ok:false, cart, errors:[{code:"OUT_OF_STOCK"}]}`) and throw only for programmer errors.
7. **Both adapters pass the same conformance suite**, and that suite is the whole insurance policy. It costs about a day: every variant covers every option; option values are display-ordered not alphabetical; `compareAtPrice` is null or strictly greater; adding an unavailable variant returns `ok:false` rather than throwing; quantity 0 removes the line; line attributes survive a round trip; `beginCheckout` on an empty cart returns `kind:"unavailable"`. When the Shopify adapter goes green, the swap is done.

**Launch mode — how he takes money before the platform is confirmed.** Ship on the local-JSON adapter with `checkout: "permalink"`. `beginCheckout()` builds `https://<shop>.myshopify.com/cart/<variantId>:1,<variantId>:2` — a real Shopify cart, zero SDK, zero token, no API version. A fully bespoke PDP and cart drawer of our own handing off to a real hosted checkout with one link. Open the store on the £1/3-month intro *now*, load the real products, and generate `catalogue.json` from real data rather than inventing it — so the owner starts learning the admin while the site is being designed.

**Capability flags so the UI can be honest instead of faking.** `capabilities: { realInventory: false, discountCodes: false, checkout: "redirect" }`. On the local adapter the discount field is disabled with "Discount codes go live with the store" rather than silently accepting nothing. The honest-empty seam is a design feature, not a placeholder.

**Media.** Hero and lookbook video on Cloudflare Stream or pre-encoded MP4+WebM on the host CDN — **not** Shopify Files, because we need orientation-discriminated sources and byte-level control. *Product* media stays in Shopify so the owner can upload it. Formats: **WebP for the scroll sequence** (decode speed is the entire bottleneck for 96 sequential decodes on a mid-range Android; AVIF decodes 5–10× slower than JPEG), **AVIF for static product photography** (bytes), H.264 High `yuv420p` for video with a WebM alternate. Never `.mov`.

**JS budget, itemised.**
- Scroll reveals: native `animation-timeline: view()` behind `@supports` (Chrome 115+, Safari 26+, Firefox still flagged in Release) + a 15-line `IntersectionObserver{once:true}` fallback. **0 KB.** These run on the compositor and cost ~0 ms of INP.
- Pinning the hourglass section: **GSAP ScrollTrigger, 27.4 KB gz, dynamic `import()`, that section only.** Free since Webflow's April 2025 change — but check `node_modules/gsap/LICENSE.md` before commercial ship; "free" is not the same as MIT, and it is a 30-second check on a client project.
- **No Lenis.** It hijacks native scroll, breaks `animation-timeline`, adds input latency by design, and overrides the user's OS scroll settings. If art direction later insists, it is desktop-only and behind `prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference`, and we then commit to GSAP's `scrollerProxy` rather than native timelines. Mixing the two is a bug factory.
- **No Three.js** (185 KB gz + 400–700 ms of main thread before first paint) and **no React Three Fiber**. The 3D flair is a composited image sequence. Blender, if used at all, is an offline renderer — it produces frames, the browser flips them.
- **No glass library.** rdev/liquid-glass-react's own README states displacement is invisible in Safari and Firefox; PallavAg's cross-browser version cannot filter live video in Safari, which is fatal given the brief. The whole Tier 2 implementation is ~60 lines of CSS. Steal kube.io's map maths, PallavAg's `userSpaceOnUse` handling, and hand-roll.

**Performance budget, enforced in CI (Lighthouse CI on a throttled Moto-G profile, build fails on regression):** LCP ≤ 2.0 s mobile (target, against the 2.5 s "good" threshold), INP ≤ 200 ms, CLS ≤ 0.05. Total page weight at first interaction on mobile ≤ 1.4 MB **excluding** the deferred sequence. The sequence loads on `load` + `requestIdleCallback`, capped at 2.5 MB mobile, and never at all under `Save-Data` or `effectiveType` 2g/3g — `Save-Data: on` is a user request, not a hint.

**UK commerce reality:** VAT registration threshold £90,000 rolling — don't register early, and display tax-inclusive so £48 means £48 at checkout. On Shopify, use Shopify Payments (Basic's 2% third-party gateway penalty makes anything else uneconomic). Start on Basic, **monthly**, not annual, until the first drop sells. Non-goals for v1, stated: customer accounts, custom checkout UI (impossible below Plus), multi-currency, subscriptions, wishlist.
anti_vibe_code:
Run against the teardown's 61-tell checklist. The decisions that fail it deliberately:

**Colour.** Zero gradients anywhere — not on a CTA, not on text, not as a hero mesh. The page ground is `#0F0F0F` measured off the client's own render, not `#0a0a0a` or `#18181b`. **There is no red on the site**, which is genuinely uncomfortable on an e-commerce build and is the clearest possible proof the palette came from the garments. The one accent is a garment colour with a written licence — time-and-stock truth only — and its 3.2:1 contrast on the ground is documented in the token file as the reason it is never body text. Tokens are named `--ot-bone`, `--ot-denim`, `--ot-quiet`, never `--primary`/`--accent`.

**Type.** Inter, Poppins, Montserrat, DM Sans, Manrope, Space Grotesk, Plus Jakarta Sans and Geist are banned by name — Trapstar and Kith are real brands whose sites read as templates for exactly this reason. Two faces, three weights, one mono. The tracking is **inverted** the way Aimé Leon Dore invert it: -0.02em at 84px, +0.15em at 10px, never the reverse, and never a wide-tracked eyebrow above every section. `tabular-nums` on every price and counter; `diagonal-fractions` on the size table so `20½"` sets properly — a one-line detail no template contains. **A Playwright test measures the rendered gap inside the OUR TIME wordmark and fails the build if it drops below 0.5em.** A build gate protecting a kerning decision is the most un-vibe-coded artefact in the repo.

**Layout.** No centred hero with a headline and two buttons. No Features/Testimonials/FAQ/CTA rhythm. No three-up card grid with length-equalised copy. No `py-24` everywhere — the vertical rhythm is 96/64/128 by editorial judgement, and section 07 has no image at all because every band having a picture is what makes a page feel generated. Radius is **0 or a full pill**, never the polite 8–16px middle, and never both on one page. Product grids use 2px gutters, not 24px — a contact sheet, not a card wall. One editorial band runs at `aspect-ratio: 2.4`, a ratio derived from a crop rather than from a scale. No logo strip, no stats band, no numbered step timeline, no badge pill above an H1, no four-column footer with a newsletter box in the last one.

**Motion.** Four named behaviours and a closed list. No custom cursor, no scroll-progress bar, no tilt cards, no count-up numbers, no typewriter, no marquee, **no stagger** — reveals in a row open simultaneously as a shutter. The one spring in the entire site is add-to-bag, which makes a commerce event feel like a transaction landing rather than a UI flourish. `prefers-reduced-motion` is wired per-behaviour with real decisions (the counter keeps ticking, because it is information, not decoration) rather than as a global `*` nuke bolted on at the end.

**Imagery.** Faces mostly absent by art direction, which is simultaneously the strongest streetwear film language and the reliable dodge for plastic-skin and glassy-eye tells. Prompts specify light physically ("single large soft key from camera left, hard falloff, no fill") rather than as a mood word. Negative prompting is replaced by a positive frame inventory, because Gemini has no negative channel and "no extra logos" reliably produces extra logos. Every `alt` is genuinely distinct.

**Copy.** No "Elevate your everyday", no "Where style meets comfort". Real numbers, real dates, real places: `DROP 001 · 11:00 FRI → 23:00 SUN`, `SOLD OUT — 23:14, SUN 12 OCT`, `Model is 6'1" / 185cm, chest 38" / 97cm, wearing M`, `1,284 ON THE LIST` — or nothing, never a rounded fake. The garment-dye disclosure ("expect up to 3% shrinkage and slight colour variation — that is the process, not a fault") is the kind of specific, slightly unflattering honesty no generated site produces.

**Glass.** One pill and one filter bar. The moment a card gets `backdrop-blur` we are in tell #23 — so no card ever does. And the differentiator is not the blur, which anyone can copy, but the two things no library gives you: the pill knowing what it is over and inverting its whole token set, and the rim specular sweeping once per page like a second hand.

**The one-line test every decision was held against:** *would this exist if the brand had a full-time art director and no AI tools?* Corteiz's 12px yellow Courier passes that test. A ticking-clock cursor does not.
risks: **The glass is the one place I am going against the entire category.** The teardown found zero streetwear brands blurring their nav — Palace's floating pill is opaque black. I have argued we can earn it with a 0.78 scrim floor and adaptive tinting, and I believe that, but it is a genuine bet against observed practice. The mitigation is that Tier 2 degrades to Tier 3 (near-opaque) with a one-line token change if it looks wrong on real content, and the scrim floor means it is already 80% of the way to opaque. Art-direct it on an actual iPhone over an actual bone product shot before signing it off.

**`position: fixed` + `backdrop-filter` recomputes the blur on every scroll frame in WebKit and does not reproduce on desktop.** It will pass local testing and can tank on the client's phone. I have mitigated it hard — 560px pill instead of a full-bleed bar (60–75% of the cost), 16px blur cap, opacity cross-fade instead of animating the radius, opaque over all video and the canvas sequence, `contain: paint`, one glass surface per viewport — but this is the single most-reported glass performance bug and it is at the centre of the brief. It must be verified with Paint Flashing on a real mid-range Android and a real iPhone, and the build does not ship if the pill region flashes green on every scroll tick.

**Tier 1 refraction may never ship on iOS, and the engine gate is a maintenance liability.** WebKit bug 245510 is still NEW, PR #68614 is `merging-blocked`, and `@supports` returns a false positive in Firefox — so the only honest detection is a user-agent sniff, which is a thing I would normally refuse to write. It needs a dated comment and a diary note to re-check bug 245510 before ship and quarterly thereafter. If refraction never arrives, the client has paid for nothing visible in Safari — which is fine only because Tier 2 carries the full identity, and that has to be genuinely true, not a claim.

**Seven SKUs do not fill a collection architecture, and the site may read thin.** I have deliberately refused to ship a filter panel over seven products, and the correction material lists a much larger confirmed range (polos, crewnecks, zip hoodies, sweatpants, jeans — ~30 colourways) that the final brief told me to design past. The types, routing and sticky bar scale, and the filter drawer switches on at >18 variants — but if the wider range lands sooner than the second drop, the homepage rhythm (one rail, one sequence, one colour bar) will need a second product band and the 'colour bar' pattern does not extend to seven garment types. That is a real re-layout, not a config change. Worth a 20-minute conversation before build starts.

**The hourglass scroll sequence is the concept's keystone and it is the hardest asset to make.** It depends on one Gemini still being genuinely good — correct print position, correct bone-on-navy contrast, correct wash mottle — plus competent hand compositing of the sand matte and a clean depth map. Depth-map quality decides everything: a mediocre photo with an excellent depth map looks good; an excellent photo with a sloppy one looks like a melting hologram. If the still or the matte is not right, the whole section has to be cut, and the homepage loses its single piece of 3D flair. Budget hand-touching the depth map where the shoulder silhouette meets the backdrop.

**The countdown is a commitment the client has to keep.** A drop that closes at 23:00 Sunday must actually close, and the site must actually go to a closed state with struck sizes. If the owner leaves stock live after the timer expires, the mechanic is exposed as theatre and it poisons every future drop. This is a business-operations dependency, not a design one, and it is the most likely way this direction fails in practice. It also means the drop window must be content-managed from day one so he can move it himself — hardcoding it is how a countdown becomes an embarrassment.

**AI faces plus an AI wordmark plus AI video is three fidelity risks stacked.** The observed failure modes are real: letterspaced word spaces collapse ('OUR TIME' → 'OURTIME'), and dark garments default to dark ink and lose print contrast. I have prompted against both explicitly and moved the wordmark out of generation entirely (inline SVG, never rendered by a model), but the OT monogram on the thigh and the hourglass on the back are still model-rendered and will need a real rejection rate. Iterating on a previous output is the reliable repair; re-prompting the original is not. Budget QA attention, not API spend — the money is trivial (~£13 pilot, ~£70 full) and the attention is not.

**Astro SSR adds an operational surface the owner cannot maintain.** Static hosting would be simpler, but metaobjects and PDP SEO both need a server. That means a runtime, an edge deployment, a quarterly Shopify API-version bump, and a person who can do it. The mitigation is that the version string lives in exactly one file and the adapter is behind a conformance suite — but 'the cousin cannot do this bit' is a permanent, honest cost of going headless, and it should be written into the handover note alongside the one-page 'what you can change yourself' guide rather than discovered later.

**If the owner turns out to want to re-lay-out pages himself weekly, this architecture is wrong and a custom Liquid theme genuinely wins.** That is the one honest argument against the whole recommendation. It needs to be a gate, asked explicitly before the ContentAdapter is built, not a discovery in month three.
